answer: Dataclasses fit poorly when: 1) construction needs real logic (validation, coercion, cross-field side effects) - __post_init__ can hold it, but once it gets complex an explicit __init__ reads better. 2) You want identity, not value, equality - dataclasses auto-generate __eq__ over all fields, wrong for mutable stateful objects like connections or controllers; you'd need eq=False anyway. 3) Mutable defaults require field(default_factory=...), an easy trap if forgotten. 4) Inheritance gets awkward: a subclass can't add a field without a default after a base field that has one (kw_only=True in 3.10+ helps). 5) The class is mostly behavior with few stored attributes - little boilerplate saved, but you still inherit __eq__/__repr__ you may not want. 6) You need another framework's base or metaclass (Pydantic, SQLAlchemy models, Django models) - combining @dataclass with those is fragile. 7) You need real runtime type validation - dataclasses only annotate types, they don't enforce them.

No - train_test_split isn't intrinsically required for PCA. PCA is unsupervised: it only uses X (your y columns don't affect fitting it) and finds directions of maximum variance in whatever data you give it; it doesn't learn a predictive mapping. If your goal is purely exploratory - visualizing variance structure, or clustering all your data with KMeans - fitting PCA on the full dataset is fine. A split matters only when PCA is a preprocessing step inside a pipeline you're evaluating for generalization (e.g., PCA plus a classifier, or checking whether KMeans clusters agree with held-out y labels): then fit the scaler and PCA on the training set only, and transform, never re-fit, the test set with those same parameters, to avoid leakage. Two points regardless of splitting: always standardize your 100 columns before PCA since it's variance-based and unscaled features dominate; and with 3000+ rows and 100 columns you have plenty of samples, so dimensionality isn't itself a concern.

Likely cause: output.output_buffer().dim(...).set_stride(...) only sets a scheduling-level estimate on the buffer wrapper, not a hard constraint baked into the compiled pipeline's argument contract, so at runtime, when you pass a genuinely interleaved (AoS) buffer, Halide's bounds/stride check still expects the default planar layout (stride(0)==1) and rejects it. The C++ Output<Buffer<>> API supports .dim() directly for declaring such constraints, not just via output_buffer(); Python's OutputBuffer should mirror this in recent Halide releases, so if yours truly lacks .dim(), upgrading is likely the fix. Set the stride/extent constraints on self.output directly inside generate(), matching input exactly, and make sure both input and output constraints are declared before compilation. Also verify the JS-side halide_buffer_t strides you construct match the compiled constraint exactly (3 for dim 0, 1 for dim 2); any mismatch between compiled constraints and the buffer passed at call time triggers precisely this runtime violation. This API is version-sensitive, so sharing your exact Halide version would help narrow it down further.

Most likely either the brand list loads asynchronously (a fixed time.sleep(5) fires too early) or autovit.ro serves different markup to headless/bot-like clients - many sites detect headless Chrome and return a cookie-consent or interstitial page instead of real content. Try: 1) replace time.sleep with WebDriverWait(driver, 15).until(EC.presence_of_all_elements_located(...)) on the actual brand-list selector; 2) inspect the live page's DOM in devtools to get the current class name, since selectors go stale as sites redesign and whatever the old code targeted may no longer exist; 3) handle the cookie-consent banner most Romanian sites show on first load, which can block content behind an overlay even though it's present in the DOM; 4) log len(driver.page_source) or save a screenshot to confirm real content arrived before parsing with BeautifulSoup; 5) if the page is empty even after waiting, the site may be blocking Selenium via navigator.webdriver detection, so try undetected-chromedriver. Since your snippet is cut off, first verify the exact selector against today's live page source.

TIMER() is an async function, so stats_timer = TIMER() only builds a coroutine object; nothing runs yet, which is why sending it just prints its repr. You must schedule it and have it send messages itself, not return a value to print later. Fix: give TIMER a channel argument and replace every print(...) with await channel.send(str(value)); then launch it as a background task instead of calling it and sending the object: asyncio.create_task(TIMER(ctx.channel)) inside your !my_timer handler, guarding with a flag so it can't be started twice, or start it once in on_ready via self.loop.create_task(TIMER(channel)) if it should run for the bot's whole lifetime. Since TIMER is an infinite while True loop, awaiting it directly would block your command handler forever; create_task lets it run concurrently while the bot keeps handling other commands. In short: schedule the coroutine with create_task, and move the actual Discord-sending logic inside TIMER itself.

Canvas.raster() is the likely culprit - unlike points()/quadmesh(), it resamples onto a regular output grid, and depending on version its dask path can trigger a large intermediate materialization or implicit rechunk rather than a truly lazy per-chunk reduction across a 150k x 90k array. Try: 1) spin up an explicit dask.distributed.Client with a per-worker memory_limit so Dask spills to disk instead of blowing past RAM, since the default threaded scheduler has no backpressure; 2) open its dashboard link to see exactly which task balloons; 3) shrink chunk size, since 8192x8192 is large - try 1024-2048; 4) pre-downsample with xarray's .coarsen() before calling Canvas, since raster's job is essentially resampling anyway; 5) check whether irregular or non-monotonic coordinates are forcing extra full-array work; 6) as a workaround, try Canvas.quadmesh() instead of raster() if applicable, since it has a more mature dask code path. This looks like a known raster+dask scaling pain point rather than a mistake in your usage.

Classic Python pitfall: def __init__(self, children={}, ...) uses a mutable default argument. That {} dict literal is created exactly once, when the function is defined, and shared by every Trie instance that doesn't explicitly pass children, so keys inserted into one node's default dict leak into all future Trie() calls that rely on the default, across test cases that reuse the same class or process. That's exactly your symptom: a fresh Trie() picks up 'app'/'apple' left over from the previous test. Fix: def __init__(self, children=None, ...): self.children = {} if children is None else children. Never use a mutable object (list, dict, set) as a default argument value; use None and create the mutable object inside the function body instead. This also explains why it works standalone or in the debugger: a fresh process or module import resets the default dict, but LeetCode's judge apparently reuses the same loaded module/class across grouped test cases without reimporting, so the shared default persists between them.

This leans more toward a discussion/opinion topic than a debuggable question, so it might also fit r/MachineLearning or Kaggle's forums - but concretely: your self-play evolutionary idea can work but is slow and sample-inefficient starting from random weights. Two better-trodden paths: 1) AlphaZero-style - a policy/value neural network combined with Monte Carlo Tree Search during self-play; Connect 4 is small enough that this converges in reasonable time on one machine, and open-source reference implementations exist to study rather than starting from scratch. 2) Since Connect 4 is a fully solved game (first player wins with perfect play), minimax plus alpha-beta search with a precomputed or hand-crafted evaluation function gives a strong, fast opponent or baseline with no training needed, useful for benchmarking your network. For pure RL, self-play Q-learning/DQN with an experience replay buffer and reward only at terminal states (+1/-1/0) converges faster than two randomly-initialized nets just competing without search. Kaggle's 'ConnectX' competition has many public solutions worth studying.

By default pytest doesn't strictly guarantee running files in the exact order given on the command line once collection and plugins get involved, and the warning you're seeing points at the real problem: pytest.mark.run(order=N) is a marker from the pytest-ordering plugin, which is either not installed, or you're actually using pytest-order instead (its marker is pytest.mark.order(N), not run(...)). An unregistered custom mark is silently accepted but does nothing except warn. Fix: pip install pytest-order and switch to @pytest.mark.order(1), @pytest.mark.order(2), etc. - pytest-ordering is old and unmaintained, pytest-order is its maintained successor and the modern recommended approach. If you'd rather not add a plugin dependency, add a conftest.py with a pytest_collection_modifyitems(session, config, items) hook that manually reorders the collected items list by filename in your desired sequence; this gives full control without relying on any ordering plugin, which matters since AWS Batch environments sometimes have subtly different installed packages than local dev.

This pattern - long stable run, then StepCount frozen with no exceptions, then spontaneous recovery after 20-30 min - looks less like an ML-Agents/Python-trainer bug and more like a GPU-level stall in the RenderTexture readback path (Camera to RenderTexture to CPU-side pixel copy), possibly compounded by Windows TDR (Timeout Detection and Recovery) firing when the GPU command queue backs up under many parallel environments, with the driver resetting and things resuming afterward. Worth checking: 1) Windows Event Viewer for TDR/display-driver-reset events around stall times; 2) whether the readback uses synchronous ReadPixels vs AsyncGPUReadback, since synchronous reads across many parallel envs can serialize and back up badly; 3) whether reducing parallel environment count or RenderTexture resolution changes the stall interval; 4) updating GPU drivers. Since your own testing already isolated it to RenderTexture-based visual observations, this looks like a known class of issue - search or file against the ML-Agents GitHub repo with your exact versions, since this is engine-level behavior that's hard to fully diagnose from code alone.

Don't split on every comma - compound names themselves contain commas, but the trailing fields (RT, Score, Area, the area value, tR (min), RT again) have a fixed, recognizable shape. Anchor on that fixed suffix instead, letting the compound name match greedily up to it:
import re
pattern = re.compile(r'^\s*(.+?)\s*,([\d.]+),(\d+),Area,([\d.]+),tR \(min\),([\d.]+)\s*$')
m = pattern.match(line)
name, rt, score, area, tr = m.groups()
Using .+? (non-greedy) for the name combined with the anchored, fixed trailing pattern lets re backtrack correctly until the rest matches, regardless of how many commas appear inside the name itself. This is far more robust than str.split(',') or a naive greedy regex. If some lines omit fields or use slightly different spacing, adjust the optional whitespace (\s*) and field order, or make trailing groups optional with (?:...)? where needed.

This is almost certainly an interpreter mismatch: pygame got installed into one Python environment (e.g., system Python via pip3, or a different venv) while VS Code is running your script with a different interpreter that doesn't have it. Steps: 1) open a terminal in your project and activate the venv: source venv/bin/activate (prompt should show (venv)); 2) confirm which python3 and which pip3 both point inside that venv folder; 3) run pip install pygame, or python3 -m pip install pygame, inside that active venv; 4) in VS Code press Cmd+Shift+P, run Python: Select Interpreter, and explicitly choose the interpreter path inside your venv, not the system one - VS Code also shows this in the bottom-right status bar, click it to switch; 5) verify from that same terminal with python3 -c 'import pygame'. On Apple Silicon Macs also make sure you have a reasonably recent pygame version (pip install --upgrade pygame), since older releases lacked arm64 wheels and could fail to install cleanly.

No, this won't crash your Flask app or throw exceptions under normal operation. Opening a file in append mode ('a') on POSIX (Linux/macOS) gives OS-level atomic writes for each individual write() call as long as the message is reasonably short (well under the OS atomic-write threshold, typically a few KB), because O_APPEND writes are serialized at the kernel level. So with 4 concurrent workers/threads you'll get interleaved log lines (messages arriving out of the chronological order you might expect) but not corrupted or garbled bytes within a single line, and no exceptions. Real risks: 1) if any single log message is unusually large (multi-KB+), interleaving mid-write becomes possible, producing a genuinely mangled line; 2) opening and closing the file on every call adds overhead that scales badly under heavy concurrent load; 3) on Windows the guarantees are weaker. Worst case here is messy or out-of-order logs, not a crash. For correctness and less overhead, use Python's logging module with a process-safe handler (e.g., concurrent-log-handler) instead of raw per-call file opens.

This is a reasonable, standard pattern (EnsembleRetriever combining a dense vector retriever with BM25Retriever), but a few issues will hurt it in practice: 1) rebuilding BM25Retriever.from_documents(...) from chroma.get() on every single query is expensive, since it retokenizes and reconstructs the whole in-memory BM25 index per request; build and cache it once, e.g. at startup or after ingestion, and reuse the retriever object instead of recreating it inside hybrid_search. 2) You need an actual EnsembleRetriever combining both, e.g. EnsembleRetriever(retrievers=[chroma.as_retriever(search_kwargs={'k': k}), bm25_retriever], weights=[0.5, 0.5]), adjusting weights to tune vector vs keyword influence. 3) BM25Retriever is pure in-memory and won't scale well past tens of thousands of documents; for larger corpora consider a store with native hybrid sparse+dense support instead. 4) Make sure metadata/IDs align between both retrievers' Document objects so EnsembleRetriever's fusion merges and deduplicates correctly rather than treating equivalent chunks as distinct results.

Your A matrix looks fine, but b has a real bug. The correct least-squares closest-point-to-lines formula is A = sum_i(I - d_i d_i^T), b = sum_i(I - d_i d_i^T) p_i = sum_i(p_i - d_i * (d_i . p_i)), where d_i . p_i is a per-line scalar dot product. Your code instead computes np.dot(direction, np.dot(direction.T, position)): direction.T @ position mixes every direction with every position across the whole array into a 3x3 matrix summing cross terms between different lines i and j, then direction @ that mixes them again. That's not equivalent to the per-line scalar dot products you actually need, and it produces the wrong, far-off point. Fix by computing row-wise dot products explicitly:
dots = np.sum(direction * position, axis=1)
b = np.sum(position - direction * dots[:, None], axis=0)
point = np.linalg.pinv(A).dot(b)
This should land near [0, 0, ~20] as you expected. Also double-check your direction vectors are unit-normalized, since the A formula assumes that - they look close to it already in your sample data.

This is a Windows file-locking issue in uv, the installer uvx uses, not really a Home Assistant-specific problem: something is holding pywin32-311.data's DLL open when uv tries to clean up its temp build directory, most commonly antivirus/Defender real-time scanning, Explorer previewing that folder, or a leftover uvx/python process from a prior failed attempt still running. Try in order: 1) fully quit Claude Desktop and check Task Manager for lingering uvx.exe/python.exe processes, end them; 2) clear uv's cache by running uv cache clean, or manually delete the uv cache folder under your Local AppData; 3) temporarily exclude that uv cache folder from antivirus real-time scanning - an AV locking a newly-written DLL mid-extraction is a very common cause of exactly this 'process cannot access the file' error on Windows; 4) run uvx ha-mcp directly in a plain terminal outside Claude to confirm it completes cleanly there, which tells you whether it's Claude's launch sandboxing or a systemic uv/AV conflict. Once uvx succeeds standalone, retry Connect inside Claude Desktop.

Yes, this is bad practice - it violates the Liskov Substitution Principle. Method parameters should be contravariant in overrides (same type or wider), not narrower: any code written against the base type Foo is entitled to call print_stuff with any List[str], and that must keep working for every subclass, including Bar and Baz. If Bar/Baz narrow the accepted type, a type checker like mypy will flag the override as unsound or incompatible with the supertype, and generic code looping over mixed Foo subclasses and calling print_stuff can pass a value one particular subclass isn't actually prepared to handle correctly. Return types are the opposite case - they may legitimately be narrowed (covariant) in a subclass. If Bar and Baz genuinely only make sense with fixed-length input, they probably shouldn't inherit Foo's interface at all: prefer composition, a differently named method, or a Protocol tailored to each, rather than an override that secretly tightens the contract callers rely on. Runtime Python won't stop you either way since annotations aren't enforced, but static analysis and API correctness both suffer.

file_ids on messages.create() was removed when OpenAI moved the Assistants API to v2; attaching files to a message now goes through the attachments parameter instead, with an explicit list of which tool(s) should use each file:
message = client.beta.threads.messages.create(
    thread_id=thread.id,
    role='user',
    content='Here is the HTML content for the seminar page.',
    attachments=[{'file_id': file.id, 'tools': [{'type': 'file_search'}]}]
)
Use {'type': 'code_interpreter'} instead if that tool should access the file. Also make sure the Assistant itself has the matching tool enabled, and for file_search a vector store configured, since attaching a file to a message doesn't implicitly enable a tool that isn't turned on for the assistant. This is a real, fairly recent breaking change in the API/SDK, not a version-install issue, so old tutorials or ChatGPT's own suggestions referencing file_ids describe the deprecated Assistants v1 shape.
